## Objects, Data Structures, and Importing Data

### Session 2

Today we will connect three important ideas:

``` text
objects → data structures → external data files
```

By the end, we should be able to create simple R objects, understand the basic structure of datasets, and import data from CSV and Excel files.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## R works with objects

Most of the time, we give R a value and store it in an object.

``` r
number_of_cameras <- 12

species <- "Raccoon"

camera_active <- TRUE
```

The object name is on the left.

The value is on the right.

``` text
object_name <- value
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why create objects?

Without an object, R gives us a result but does not save it.

``` r
2 + 2
```

But if we assign the result:

``` r
result <- 2 + 2
```

we can use it again later.

``` r
result
result * 10
```

::: fragment
Objects allow us to build an analysis step by step.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Naming objects

Good object names make code easier to understand.

``` r
x <- 25
```

works, but this is more informative:

``` r
number_of_cameras <- 25
```

During this course, we will mostly use `snake_case`.

``` r
camera_days
number_of_detections
survey_data
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

![](/images/module-02/codingetiquete.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A few naming rules

Object names:

- should not begin with a number
- should not contain spaces
- should avoid special characters
- should avoid accents
- should not reuse common function names

R is case-sensitive:

``` r
camera_data
Camera_data
```

are different names.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Basic object types

R can store different types of values.

| Type          | Example     |
|---------------|-------------|
| numeric       | `25`        |
| character     | `"Raccoon"` |
| logical       | `TRUE`      |
| missing value | `NA`        |

::: fragment
A number inside quotation marks is not a number.
:::

``` r
fake_number <- "25"
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Operators

Arithmetic operators return numbers.

``` r
10 + 5
10 - 5
10 * 5
10 / 5
10 ^ 2
```

Relational operators return `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

``` r
10 > 5
10 == 5
10 != 5
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Functions

Functions perform specific tasks.

Most functions look like this:

``` text
function_name(object)
```

For example:

``` r
class(25)
class("25")
class(TRUE)
```

Functions can also use arguments:

``` r
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Help is part of using R

You do not need to memorize every function.

Use the help system:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| 
?round
```

``` r
```

or:

```{r}
#| eval: false

help(round)

```

``` r
```

::: fragment
Learning R is not memorizing commands.\
It is learning how to find what you need.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Packages

Many functions come from packages.

The basic workflow is:

``` text
install → load → use
```

For example:

``` r
#| eval: false
#| 
install.packages("beepr")
```

``` r
library(beepr)
```

``` r
beep(sound = 8)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Code-along 1

Switch to RStudio.

Create a script called:

``` text
session-02.R
```

inside your `scripts/` folder.

Then create:

``` r
species <- "Raccoon"
station <- "CT01"
detections <- 15
```

Use R to ask:

``` r
detections > 10
class(species)
class(detections)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## From single values to data structures

So far, most objects had one value.

Real datasets have many values.

R can organize values into different structures:

- vectors
- matrices
- lists
- data frames

::: fragment
For this course, data frames will be the most important.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Vectors

![](/images/module-02/vectors.png){fig-align="center"}

A vector stores several values in one object.

``` r
detections <- c(5, 12, 8, 0, 3)
```

The function `c()` means **combine**.

We can use functions on vectors:

``` r
mean(detections)
sum(detections)
length(detections)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Vectors have one data type

A vector can contain numbers:

``` r
camera_days <- c(30, 28, 30, 25)
```

or text:

``` r
species <- c("Raccoon", "Coyote", "Bobcat")
```

or logical values:

``` r
camera_active <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

But mixing types can change the result.

``` r
mixed_vector <- c(1, 2, "Raccoon", 4)
class(mixed_vector)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

![](/images/module-02/teletubo.png){fig-align="center"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Selecting values from vectors

Use square brackets:

``` r
detections <- c(5, 12, 8, 0, 3)

detections[1]
detections[3]
detections[1:3]
detections[c(1, 3, 5)]
```

R starts counting at **1**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Selecting with conditions

Relational operators work with vectors.

``` r
detections > 5
```

This returns one logical value for each element.

We can use that condition to select values:

``` r
detections[detections > 5]
```

::: fragment
This is the basic idea behind filtering data.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Matrices

A matrix has two dimensions:

``` text
rows × columns
```

![](/images/module-02/Matrix.png){fig-align="center"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Example:

``` r
detection_matrix <- matrix(
  1:12,
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 3
)

detection_matrix
```

To select values:

``` r
detection_matrix[row, column]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why should we care about matrices?

Camera-trap detection histories often look like matrices.

``` text
        occasion_1  occasion_2  occasion_3
CT01         0           1           0
CT02         1           0           0
CT03         0           0           1
```

Rows are sites or stations.

Columns are sampling occasions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Lists

![](/images/module-02/Litst.png){fig-align="center"}

Lists can store different kinds of objects together.

``` r
camera_information <- list(
  station = "CT01",
  active = TRUE,
  detections = 25,
  species = c("Raccoon", "Coyote", "Bobcat")
)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Access elements with:

``` r
camera_information$station
camera_information$species
```

::: fragment
Many R functions return lists.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Data frames

A data frame is a rectangular table.

It has:

- rows
- columns

It looks similar to an Excel spreadsheet.

But unlike a matrix, each column can have a different type.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Data frames

![](/images/module-02/dataframe.png){fig-align="center"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Creating a data frame

``` r
station <- c("CT01", "CT02", "CT03", "CT04")

habitat <- c("Forest", "Forest", "Pasture", "Pasture")

camera_days <- c(30, 28, 30, 27)

active <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

camera_data <- data.frame(
  station,
  habitat,
  camera_days,
  active
)

camera_data
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Rows and columns

In most ecological datasets:

``` text
rows    = observations
columns = variables
```

For example:

| station | habitat | camera_days | active |
|---------|---------|------------:|--------|
| CT01    | Forest  |          30 | TRUE   |
| CT02    | Forest  |          28 | TRUE   |
| CT03    | Pasture |          30 | FALSE  |

Each row is one camera station.

Each column is one variable.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Inspecting data frames

Before analyzing data, inspect it.

``` r
head(camera_data)
str(camera_data)
dim(camera_data)
names(camera_data)
```

Ask:

- How many rows?
- How many columns?
- Are the column names correct?
- Are numeric columns actually numeric?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Selecting from a data frame

Use `$` to select a column:

``` r
camera_data$station
camera_data$camera_days
```

Use `[row, column]` to select by position:

``` r
camera_data[1, 2]
camera_data[1, ]
camera_data[, 2]
```

Later we will learn more readable tools with `dplyr`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Code-along 2

Create this data frame:

``` r
station <- c("CT01", "CT02", "CT03")

habitat <- c("Forest", "Pasture", "Forest")

detections <- c(12, 5, 0)

survey_data <- data.frame(
  station,
  habitat,
  detections
)
```

Then run:

``` r
survey_data
str(survey_data)
survey_data$detections
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## External data files

Most real data will not be typed directly into R.

They will usually come from:

- Excel
- Google Sheets
- field-data software
- camera-trap metadata
- another program

So R needs to know where the file is.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Working directory

The working directory is the folder where R starts looking for files.

Check it with:

``` r
getwd()
```

Because we are using an RStudio Project, the working directory should be the main project folder.

``` text
intro-r-course/
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Relative paths

If your file is here:

``` text
intro-r-course/
│
├── data/
│   └── camera_data.csv
│
├── scripts/
└── outputs/
```

you can refer to it as:

``` text
data/camera_data.csv
```

::: fragment
This is better than using a full path from your own computer.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## CSV files

CSV means:

``` text
Comma-Separated Values
```

A CSV is a plain-text table.

``` text
station,species,detections,camera_days
CT01,Raccoon,12,30
CT02,Coyote,5,28
CT03,Bobcat,8,30
```

CSV files are simple, portable, and easy to read in R.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Importing a CSV file

Base R:

``` r
camera_data <- read.csv("data/camera_data.csv")
```

Tidyverse / readr:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

camera_data2 <- read_csv("data/camera_data.csv")
```

The important pattern is:

``` text
object <- read_function("path/to/file")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Importing Excel files

To read Excel files, use `readxl`.

``` r
library(readxl)

camera_data3 <- read_excel("data/camera_data.xlsx")
```

If the file has multiple sheets:

``` r
excel_sheets("data/camera_data.xlsx")
```

``` r
camera_data3 <- read_excel(
  "data/camera_data.xlsx",
  sheet = "camera_records"
)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Always inspect imported data

After importing:

``` r
head(camera_data)
str(camera_data)
dim(camera_data)
names(camera_data)
```

Do not assume the file imported correctly just because R did not show an error.

::: fragment
Trust, but verify.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Common import problems

Most import errors are simple:

- wrong file name
- wrong folder
- different capitalization
- missing package
- file not saved in the project
- Excel changed dates or values

Useful checks:

``` r
file.exists("data/camera_data.csv")
list.files("data")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now import the Excel file.

``` r

  "data/camera_data.xlsx"

```

Check the sheets:

``` r

```

``` r

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exporting data

To save a CSV from R:

``` r
write.csv(
  camera_data,
  "outputs/camera_data_clean.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

With readr:

``` r
write_csv(
  camera_data,
  "outputs/camera_data_clean.csv"
)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Keep raw data separate

A useful structure:

``` text
intro-r-course/
│
├── data/
│   └── camera_data.csv
│
├── scripts/
│   └── session-02.R
│
└── outputs/
    └── camera_data_clean.csv
```

`data/` contains original or input files.

`outputs/` contains files created by your analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Main idea

R work often follows this pattern:

``` text
create objects
      ↓
organize values
      ↓
import data
      ↓
inspect data
      ↓
work with data
      ↓
export results
```

The details take practice.

But this workflow will appear again and again.
